data.text/markdown:
Statistical paradoxes are everywhere: the inspection paradox

An interactive companion to marimo's video "Statistical Paradoxes Are Everywhere".
A teacher and every student in the same room write down the same number: how many students are in this class. Repeat this for every class in the school. Then average the teachers' notes and average the students' notes. The two averages disagree, by a lot.
This is the inspection paradox. When the way you sample depends on the thing you measure, your average quietly changes. In this notebook you'll replay three riddles from the video in simulation, which is the mental replay technique the video recommends, and then try a bonus riddle about your bus being "always late".

data.text/markdown: Lock in an answer above. Section 1 will show you who was right.

Riddle 1 · The teacher and the students

Each class contributes one teacher's note, but n students' notes, and every one of those notes says n. A class of 100 gets 100 votes from its students and still only one from its teacher. A class of 1 gets one vote either way. Averaging over teachers gives the plain mean. Averaging over students gives a size-biased mean: ||[\bar n_{\text{teacher}} = E[n] \qquad\qquad \bar n_{\text{student}} = \frac{\sum n\cdot n}{\sum n} = \frac{E[n^2]}{E[n]} = E[n] + \frac{\operatorname{Var}(n)}{E[n]}||]The gap is exactly ||(\operatorname{Var}(n)/E[n]||). If every class had the same size, there would be no paradox. Press ▶ play to watch classes form one by one. Then press ⏩ to run it fast.

data.text/markdown:
Riddle 2 · "How many siblings do you have?"

Now the teacher keeps their own number to themselves and only asks the students. That seems fair: one student, one answer. But it still doesn't tell you how many children families have. Two things go wrong:
  • A family with k children sends k representatives into the room. This is the size bias from Riddle 1 again.
  • A family with 0 children sends no one. That family is invisible to anyone surveying the room.
Riddle 1 was distorted by the heavy end. This one is also distorted by an invisible zero end.

🧩 Challenge from the video: can you reverse it?

You only get to survey the room (the red bars). Can you reconstruct the parents' distribution (blue)? Each family with ||(k||) kids shows up ||(k||) times, so dividing by ||(k||) should undo the weighting: ||[P_{\text{family}}(k) \propto \frac{P_{\text{room}}(k)}{k} \quad (k \ge 1)||]Toggle the switch to try it. Then look closely at the k = 0 bar.

Riddle 3 · One day of players vs. everyone so far

The analytics trap. Imagine an online game (the video uses real World of Warcraft logs). You want to know how many hours per day a typical player plays. You could look at:
  • 🔵 everyone who played during a period (for example, "all players so far"), or
  • 🔴 everyone who played on a single survey day.
Same game, same players, same metric. Which group plays more hours per day? Make a guess first. Our simulated players come in two types, as in the video: tourists try the game once for a short session and never return, and regulars come back day after day.

data.text/markdown:
Bonus · Why is your bus always late?

This is a classic from Allen Downey's Probably Overthinking It, which the video recommends. Buses arrive on average every 10 minutes. You show up at a random time. How long do you wait? "Half the gap, so 5 minutes" is only right if the buses are perfectly regular. You are far more likely to arrive during a long gap, because long gaps cover more of the clock. That's the size bias again, this time in time instead of in people: ||[E[\text{wait}] = \frac{E[g^2]}{2\,E[g]} = \frac{E[g]}{2}\left(1 + \mathrm{CV}^2\right)||]Click on the timeline to arrive at the stop, or drop 200 random passengers.

data.text/markdown:
Spot the paradox

The video's real promise: once you know it, you'll notice it everywhere. For each scenario, does the inspection paradox bias the number?

data.text/html:
Your friends have more friends than you do, on average.
Surveying current prisoners gives a longer average sentence than the court records.
On the highway, most cars seem to overtake you or be overtaken; few drive your speed.
The average of 1,000 fair die rolls is about 3.5.
Gym members you meet at the gym work out more often than the average member.
Patients in a hospital today have longer stays than the average admission.

data.text/markdown: Answer, then flip the switch.

Recap: how to defend yourself

Riddle Who gets over-sampled Who goes missing
Teacher vs students big classes (n notes each) –
Siblings big families childless families (zero kids, zero answers)
Players per day heavy, returning users one-off tourists pile up in long periods
Bus stop long gaps short gaps
  1. Mental replay: simulate the process that created each row. Who got to write a note, and how many?
  2. Check the extremes: a class of 1 vs. a class of 100. A family of 0. A player who quits after 10 minutes.
  3. Name your unit of averaging: per class, per student, per player, per player-day? Each one answers a different question.
